Inspired by the significant advancements in supervised learning with spiking neural networks, researchers are now exploring unsupervised spike-based learning techniques. We propose a novel, biologically plausible learning algorithm called Backpropagation Through Time for Spikes (BPTTS), which builds upon the classic Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm for supervised learning. The proposed BPTTS maintains the same efficient numerical optimization characteristics while adapting for discrete time sequences and spiking events. Furthermore, our method shares similarities with popular deep reinforcement learning techniques such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). We evaluate the effectiveness of BPTTS on two distinct sequence learning datasets and demonstrate its performance in comparison to established spike-based learning methods.

This report serves as a comprehensive overview, detailing the progress of the 
2021 OOV challenge and incorporating insights from participant feedback and expert 
consultations. The OOV challenge aimed to address the OOD (Out-Of-Distribution) 
issue in NLP tasks, specifically focusing on how models handle words lacking 
entries in their initial training dictionaries. Although the 2021 competition did not 
yield a clear winner due to non-compliant participant submissions, the report 
preserves the original problem definition and provides a summary of the receiving 
submissions.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with these equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to determine the accuracy of these expansions, taking into account the original differential equations' uncertainty and approximations involved. This investigation specifically focuses on a particular type of chaos expansions known as GALERKI, which is applied to the Kepler problem to assess its reliability and precision.

In various industries such as process control, food processing, and self-healing systems, detecting and isolating shifts in hidden patterns is crucial to prevent widespread damage. Unlike traditional approaches that focus on overall pattern assessment, this work aims to identify individual underlying components that have deviated. We introduce a novel framework for identifying changes within partially observable sequences by analyzing subspace projections of related data. This approach is enhanced by a non-parametric method for accurately pinpointing the source of the shift within the projected subspace. Extensive simulation testing validates our proposed model and compares it to established techniques.

We utilize the vast database of galaxy evolution, specifically the stellar population synthesis models and a comprehensive abundance database, to create detailed star formation histories for numerous dwarf galaxies. By applying single-zone chemical abundance models, we are able to measure key metal production factors for these galaxies. Our analysis reveals distinct patterns in the production of heavy elements, specifically helium-4 and metallicity, that can be used to understand mass distribution trends in dwarf galaxy populations. Furthermore, our results indicate a clear link between a galaxy's mass and its metal production, supporting existing research, while also revealing a possible exception in the low-mass galaxy Reticulum II. Additionally, our study provides further evidence supporting the widespread occurrence of multiple early star formation episodes in dwarf galaxies, as well as the presence of two distinct types of supernovae explosions, including type Ia and core-collapse supernovae, that produce different elements at varying abundance levels.

Given a profinite group G, we define the homotopy orbit spectrum as VG = G × G Map(G, BZ) ∼ ∐[G,G] BZ, establishing that it serves as a G-spectrum. Additionally, we identify VG with the completion of Z[G] pt, where the subscript 'pt' denotes localizing at Charleston elements. This construction has practical applications in the study of profinite groups.

A recent breakthrough in vision-based document extraction has the potential to replace traditional OCR, but current models require an excessive amount of labeled data to achieve high accuracy, making them impractical for widespread use. In this research, we demonstrate that these costs can be significantly reduced by leveraging existing data for improved results. The study proposes an adaptable approach to batch both extraction and formatting correction tasks, allowing for the efficient allocation of labeling resources. By sharing labeling efforts across related tasks, the required labels for each individual task are dramatically decreased. The research showcases its effectiveness through an actual use case involving invoices and provides comprehensive analysis to justify its logic.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained interest due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a III-Arside semiconductor. By employing a combination of theoretical and experimental approaches, researchers have investigated the electronic structure and magnetic behavior at the EuS/InAs interface. Specifically, density functional and many-body calculations using both supercell and slab models were conducted to study the interface's properties. These studies indicated the development of a gap state and magnetic moments on the EuS side of the interface, in agreement with experimental findings from photoemission spectroscopy. Furthermore, analysis of the spin-orbit coupling and interfacial charge transfer revealed the origin of the observed resonance signal observed in the experiments. By exploring different bonding configurations between EuS and InAs, researchers discovered that the electronic and magnetic properties at the interface are significantly influenced by the manner in which the atoms from the two materials bond.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are now preferred for object detection and segmentation tasks, but their large size hinders them on mobile devices and in memory-constrained settings. Weight pruning has emerged as a solution to reduce model size, but previous methods have drawbacks - they either compromise model accuracy or require retraining from scratch after pruning. A newer approach, Knowledge Distillation, can aid in pruning, but it typically requires the pruned model to be reinitialized from a dense state, negating the purpose of pruning. There has been a lack of research on combining pruning and knowledge distillation in a single unified framework. Our proposed ClickTrain approach addresses this gap by efficiently and accurately integrating pruning and knowledge distillation, allowing the pruned model to be trained directly from a sparse state without needing to reinitialize from a dense state. Our solution involves a novel and efficient form of sparsity-aware activation gradient computation that enables backpropagation in a pruned model without requiring full activation vectors. This leads to a significant reduction in computational and memory requirements during training. Our experiments show that ClickTrain achieves a substantial reduction in model size (up to 13x), a significant decrease in memory usage (up to 8.5x), and a notable increase in model accuracy (an average of 6.3% compared to a pruned model initialized from zeros), all without requiring the model to be reinitialized and with only a minor loss in accuracy compared to a dense model.

Recent breakthroughs in detector technology have enabled the detection of gravitational waves produced by merging compact objects, including neutron star and black hole mergers. The analysis of these signals offers a unique opportunity to deepen our understanding of celestial bodies such as neutron stars and black holes. Their mass distributions, however, remain largely unknown. Manually examining the vast number of gravitational waves generated by each event is impractical, and so, developing algorithms to automatically extract essential information from these signals is crucial. In this study, we introduce a deep learning approach using a Convolutional Neural Network to classify the gravitational waves resulting from black hole and neutron star mergers by identifying their distinct binary component masses. The method is based on an initial phase where the network segments the time-series signal into its individual components and then assesses their properties. Our findings indicate that a Convolutional Neural Network can effectively identify the mass ratios of merging black holes with an accuracy of 97% and 90% for low signal-to-noise ratios of 20 and 10, respectively. Although our model performed better for neutron star merger analysis, its potential applications are limited due to the vast number of possible mass combinations.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant planet, which was identified through the community follow-up to the TESS mission's data collection. The planet, which has a mass similar to that of Jupiter, orbits a star approximately 10.3 billion years old called TOI-5542, which is located in the constellation of Scorpius. The planet's radius is approximately 1.23 times that of Jupiter, which indicates it has a primarily hydrogen-helium composition. Through a detailed analysis of the star's properties, researchers found that TOI-5542 has a metallicity significantly lower than average, which suggests this planet may have formed through a high-accretion rate of dust and rocks early in its development. The planet's orbital period is approximately 94.5 days in a slightly eccentric orbit. This new discovery adds to our understanding of planetary formation and the variety of gas giant planets that exist, particularly those with lower metallicity compositions.

We introduce an efficient algorithm for solving large Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) that generate safety-aware policies for complex scenarios with potential safety risks. Our method is inspired by the primal-dual framework and builds upon two key components: safety-reinforcing IL (Policy Improvement with IL) and safety-constrained RL (Constrained Reinforcement Learning). By integrating these components, our algorithm achieves a balance between maximizing rewards and ensuring safety, resulting in a robust and efficient solution for CMDPs.

This research paper delves into the application of offline handwritten mathematical symbol recognition, focusing on leveraging deep learning techniques to achieve high accuracy in this domain. Despite advances in handwriting recognition over the past three decades, certain groups of individuals continue to struggle with offline mathematical symbol transcription. Previous offline mathematical symbol recognition methods have been limited by their need for either handwritten or engineered features, which can be challenging especially when working with small training datasets. Our work seeks to address this challenge through the use of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) capable of learning complex patterns from large datasets, ultimately leading to improved accuracy. By developing a dataset comprising 300,000 mathematical symbols drawn by 100 individuals, we have created a benchmark for evaluating the performance of mathematical symbol recognition systems across different groups. The results show that a CNN model trained on our dataset achieves 97.08% character-level accuracy, surpassing the performance of human transcribers.

We connect the growth of superconformal quantum mechanics symplectic generators to the computation of cohomology classes and their dimensions for a specific sheaf of $\mathcal{O}$ on the affine line $ \mathbb{A}^{1}$, establishing a direct relationship. Additionally, we investigate non-linear symplectic generators and their expansion in powers of the prepotential, linking this to the structure of a deformed cohomology ring and the sequence of nested inclusions of rational and algebraic deformations of the sheaf for $ \mathbb{A}^{1}$.

We conduct in-depth analysis on the behavior of the contact process using both local and global approaches on various types of random and planned networks. The contact process is an excellent model for the spread of an infectious disease or a rumor within a closed system. Our study reveals that the contact process exhibits two distinct regimes: a localized, slow spread for $\lambda < \lambda_c$ and an extensive, fast spread for $\lambda > \lambda_c$. The critical immunity $q_c$ decreases in large networks, contrary to what's observed in regular lattices. To gain further insight, we developed an equation set for $q_c$ applicable to arbitrary networks, which shows that network size significantly influences this critical point.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is a prominent approach that has achieved significant success, but it is prone to the actor-control problem, where random actions caused by exploration lead to poor performance. Notably, this issue is more apparent in continuous-action spaces. While techniques like additive Gaussian noise or trust-region methods have been employed to mitigate this problem, they have inherent drawbacks. In response, we present a novel actor-critic algorithm called Hamiltonian Actor-Critic, which combines Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with actor-critic methods to sample actions from a posterior distribution of the Hamiltonian. This approach leverages gradients to generate actions, reducing the randomity associated with exploration. By integrating HMC, our method circumvents the actor-control problem and outperforms existing methods on a range of continuous-action reinforcement learning tasks.

It's widely accepted that the Prime Number Theorem holds, and based on this, a well-known corollary suggests that the Twin Prime Conjecture must also be true. A straightforward demonstration of this corollary is presented here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing environments poses a significant challenge for advanced robotic systems. To tackle this problem, a novel two-layered control system is proposed, consisting of a high-level controller based on a behavior-based architecture and a low-level controller utilizing sensor fusion technology. The middle layer, behavior-based navigation, determines the desired robot movement, incorporating a behavioral model of exploration and navigation. In contrast, the lower layer, sensor-based movement control, generates control signals in real-time, optimizing the robot's actual movement in response to its surroundings. Specifically, the paper demonstrates the development of a real-time sonar fusion system by integrating multiple sonar modules, enabling the calculation of the robot's relative distance to obstacles and navigation space around its extension. A simulator was created to test the sonar movement control module in various environments before being successfully applied to a TurtleBot platform, as seen in the accompanying video.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune, has two distinct regions with different albedos. Our analysis of new and existing near-infrared spectra reveals that the brighter area is composed of water and ammonia ices, along with some carbonates, while the darker region contains more extensive tholins. Nereid's water-rich composition is consistent with several scenarios, including one where the satellite originates from a particular type of icy bodies in the Kuiper Belt. Water and ammonia ices are present in Nereid in varying proportions, which is similar to the composition of other objects in the Edgeworth-Kuiper Belt. Our findings also suggest that the surface of Nereid is a mix of pristine and altered ice, offering insights into its geological history.

Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a field, and let the subring $R_n(\mathbb K)$ consist of the ring of lower triangular matrices of size $n \times n$ with entries from $\mathbb K$. This research shows that affine and projective planes linked with projective lines over $R_n(\mathbb K)$ are isomorphic to the standard affine and projective planes over $\mathbb K$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the only transitive and associative representations over $R_n(\mathbb K)$ are isomorphic to the standard projective line.

This research extends the Tukey-order to measures of tail probability leakage within probabilistic circuits, utilizing preorders defined by realistic adversarial models (e.g. quantum and classical unbounded adversaries). A series of fundamental results are established, including upper and lower bounds on the complexity of leakage for specific access types, as well as sufficient conditions for individual leakage functions. Notably, it has been found that, under the query model, there exists a family of functions with exponential leakage, whereas, under the oracle model, there exists a family of functions with linear leakage.

A key challenge in improving the performance of dynamic treatment regimes has been generating pessimistic optimistic decision theory simulations efficiently. This issue is tackled by treating key model parameters under uncertainty in a Bayesian framework that aims to control the overall regime performance. By influencing the simulation's decision-making process with uncertain model parameters, the algorithm seeks to maintain a safety margin, ensuring the optimized regime's performance exceeds a certain threshold when implemented. We have developed a Bayesian approach that offers a versatile solution to this problem, along with two efficient algorithmic implementations. The first implementation leverages stochastic gradient descent, while the second applies approximate stochastic gradient descent using variational inference. Both methods enable the optimization of pessimistic optimistic decision theory simulations, leading to the identification of the most effective treatment policies.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. This framework provides new proofs of previously established dualities and gives a unified explanation for them. It also has implications for the stationary source theory of tilting bimodules and the ring order property. Additionally, the relationships between subcategories defined by tilting bimodules are shown to form a poset, with poset limits representing extensions of tilting bimodules, and this poset is shown to be autonomous under certain conditions. This poset can be used to define a Grothendieck group that represents the combinatorial nature of tilting bimodules, and this group is shown to be free.

A proposed Witting strategy for generating entanglement from spin-1/2 particles uses arrangements of lines and points, linked to the complex forms of the $E_8$ root system. We examine the success of this approach in two respects: (i) the relationship of these configurations to the points in the Cayley diagram of the Witting group, and (ii) the connection of these configurations to a specific measure of non-locality, called quantum contextuality, relevant to systems with higher numbers of anti-commuting variables.

We investigate the origin of superconductivity in two specific models based on flat bands with spin-orbital coupling and nearest-neighbor interactions. In both cases, using a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we demonstrate that superconductivity arises from an attractive pairing instability driven by inter-band interactions. Specifically, we find that superconductivity is facilitated by a particular type of pairing interaction that is sensitive to momentum and spin configuration, and is present in both models considered. In our analysis, we also examine the impact of spin-orbital coupling on superconductivity and find that it plays a crucial role in facilitating a type of pairing that is sensitive to spin, while being present in both models considered.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the 1D locally compact Abelian groups where this relationship holds, extending a theorem initially proven by Polya for the real numbers. This proof relies on a duality theorem in the dual group of the real numbers and characteristic functions of 1D locally compact Abelian groups.

Presence-absence data represents sites or observations with a list of present or absent species. This format poses challenges for data analysis, particularly when dealing with a large number of zero values. In this study, we evaluated the performance of several clustering approaches in high-dimensional presence-absence data contexts, comparing their effectiveness with or without the inclusion of zero-valued variables. Our analysis utilized simulated data sets with varying levels of species richness and presence-absence patterns, along with metrics such as the Rand index and statistical significance of clustering results. Our findings suggest that the presence of many zero-valued variables tends to fragment data clusters, reducing the accuracy of predicted group assignments and clustering evaluations. Additionally, our results indicate that the performance of different clustering methods depends on the presence of these zero-valued variables, with some methods being more affected by them than others.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention. Due to the disparity between simulated and actual depth information in real-world scenarios, most current methods combine RGB and depth data. However, this often leads to undesirable consequences such as increased complexity and decreased flexibility. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel and efficient approach that effectively integrates RGB information and leverages depth knowledge within a unified framework. By employing a dual-input encoder and shared decoder modules, our method circumvents the typical depth-based complexity and allows for greater flexibility in network design. Furthermore, our method incorporates an attention-mechanism-based decoder module to enhance performance and improve simplicity. Our experiments demonstrate superior performance on the NUS-16E, NUS-20E, NICO, and PASCAL-S datasets, with significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

This research paper details our approaches for SemEval-2019 Task 6, which focused on identifying offensive or semi-offensive posts. Our team, UM-IU@LING, applied various strategies on the provided data. Initially, we explored the performance of BERT models, including Multilingual BERT and BERT with different vocabularies, in combination with fine-tuned BERT classifiers for each task. Our findings revealed that the Multilingual BERT model, when paired with an SVM classifier, achieved a macro F1 score of 0.7946 in identifying offensive posts, while also demonstrating a macro F1 score of 0.7037 in distinguishing semi-offensive posts. Our results positioned us 68th out of 231 in the offensive identification task.

We're examining the properties of numbers formed by repeating sequences and their division. These division results can be categorized into four groups, which exhibit distinct patterns in their remainders. It's also been discovered that certain sequences produce a limitless variety of numbers within each category when divided.

Computed Tomography (CT) is a widely used medical imaging technique that captures X-ray absorption values across different energy levels. However, non-uniform and inconsistent X-ray sources can cause data corruption, which poses difficulties for subsequent processing and analysis. To address these issues, a new mathematical framework is proposed that combines low-light and noisy data into a unified optimization problem. By regulating the sensitivity of solutions to sensing conditions and energy spectra, the model ensures that reconstructed images and material decomposition results remain stable across various scanning configurations. An efficient algorithm utilizing the Chambolle-Perron process is developed to solve this optimization problem, which is then validated through numerical experiments on a variety of test cases.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data. A recent approach to address this issue involves generating synthetic labels through a trained handwriting model, yet existing methods often neglect to account for the specific intricacies of HTR. Notably, handwritten text often comprises lines with varying lengths, requiring Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence (ETI) like mechanisms to break them into individual symbols. Existing synthesis techniques either ignore these cues or rely on inaccurate estimates of the symbol boundaries, ultimately distorting the generated characters. To improve synthetic symbol quality, we propose utilizing the Ground-Truth (GT) line segmentation labels during the synthesis process. When GT labels are available, we employ them to split the image into characters through a simple yet effective cropping technique. If such labels are absent, we apply a Text Line Detection (TLD) technique to generate pseudo-GT labels, which are then used for line segmentation. Once the characters are segmented, we fine-tune a standard HTR model to concentrate on the relevant regions. Our proposed framework demonstrates superior performance on datasets with diverse formats, significantly outperforming existing baseline synthesis methods.

This paper reports on breakthroughs in the ab initio no-core shell game, specifically for the $^{48}$Ca isotope with 20 nucleons. The advancements enable the generation of highly accurate many-body wave functions through the convergence of various approximations. The study achieves this by introducing a novel symmetry-adapted near-field approximation and leveraging a novel generator coordinate method framework, 'generator chain,' for the correlated space-time T-matrix approximation. The detailed computational strategy involves the integration of different theoretical methods, including the Monte Carlo shell model, effective field theory, and lattice effective field theory. The study demonstrates that the total energy can be precisely measured with an error margin of less than one millionth, and the findings align with experimental data. The work also enables the examination of the nuclear density and radial distribution functions, thus contributing to a deeper comprehension of the intricacies within the heart of heavy nuclei.

We introduce a fundamental model in condensed matter physics, the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model, which exhibits a notable topological transition. Our discussion is focused on the educational and research potential of this model in the field of topological quantum phenomena. The SSH model is highlighted for its ability to serve as an introductory model in undergraduate and graduate coursework, as well as its value as a tool in advanced research, thanks to its simplicity and the intricate topological characteristics it embodies. Numerous modifications to the model have been explored, yielding novel ideas and applications in quantum technologies.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the unit disk.

We have derived the two-loop amplitude for five-dimensional supergravity in AdS$_5$ space-time, coupled to five-dimensional self-dual tensor gauge field, using off-shell Mellin transforms. This amplitude is suitable for a five-dimensional supersymmetric anti-de Sitter background. It complies with the principles of $N=1$ super-Poincaré invariance and satisfies the balance condition for supersymmetry, both with and without an anti-de Sitter reduction factor. This amplitude can be applied to a five-dimensional supersymmetric anti-de Sitter gravity theory, and its Mellin-transformed version is equivalent to a specific six-dimensional supersymmetric harmonic gravity theory in AdS$_5$ space-time. Furthermore, this amplitude is analogous to a corresponding two-loop amplitude in the $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory in four-dimensional Minkowski space-time, as calculated by six-dimensional supersymmetric harmonic gauge theory methods.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been limited to programing languages and applications that utilize array syntax. However, this limitation has been alleviated by Memory Array Programming, a memory-centric computation approach that allows object-oriented programming on GPUs with reduced memory access overhead. This approach employs a compact binary representation of objects to facilitate efficient memory storage and loading. To take advantage of this paradigm, it is essential to develop an efficient memory allocator that can efficiently map object arrays to device memory. Our proposed DynaSOAr allocator optimizes memory allocation and deallocation operations, including memory management, by leveraging a binary search to locate contiguous object arrays within device memory. This optimization results in a significant performance gain of up to 3.6 times over existing allocators, allowing Memory Array Programming applications to run with little to no overhead.

We develop two U(1)X models, one containing three generations of standard model fields where only one is charged, similar to the left-right model, while in the other, all charged states are heavy, inspired by the SO(10) theory. In the first model, the electric charge unification condition uniquely determines the U(1)X charge of the right-handed neutrinos, allowing us to set it to 1, which leads to the difference in U(1)X charges between left- and right-handed quarks and the difference between U(1)X and weak hypercharge being rational numbers. Furthermore, we find the U(1)X breaking scale can be around the TeV range by using the minimal supersymmetric standard model parameters. In the second model, we introduce complete multiplets of U(1)X coming from SO(10) to make all standard model fermions charged, while preserving gauge coupling unification. We find suitable discrete symmetries are necessary to generate the Majorana masses for right-handed neutrinos and the electroweak scale, while making the left-handed ones heavy. We also find the parameter space for the kinetic mixing with the weak gauge bosons that allows for neutrino related processes, such as the sub-eV scale Majoron dark matter and the production of the Majoron at LHC.

A specific measurement technique must be developed to evaluate the longitudinal
tension in superconducting straw tubes designed for future particle detectors.
Research indicates that the standard hoop-stress-based scanning method is
inapplicable due to potential material changes in straw walls. The proposed
methodology leverages a detector's magnetic field, utilizing a weak magnetic
field to detect the induced voltage on a moving probe within the straw.
Calculations and experimental results demonstrate the method's accuracy and
accounting capabilities for variables such as straw wall thickness and magnetic
field intensity. Additionally, the research explores mechanical stability across a
range of operating conditions and shows the effect of pressure on straw stability,
highlighting the importance of properly managing pressure and tension within the
straw.

In various fields, ensuring the reliability of decisions made with uncertain information is vital. The framework of probabilistic decision theory provides a foundational approach to making this assurance. However, the difficulty lies in obtaining precise upper limits on expected outcomes, as the integration of multiple random variables can lead to non-linear relationships. The application of Monte Carlo simulations and probabilistic programming does not offer strict guarantees of computation time. This research introduces a distinct approach to obtaining robust performance guarantees for expected utility values. It involves converting the utility maximization issue into a more manageable optimization problem, one that can be solved more efficiently by leveraging the structure of probabilistic circuits.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position. Notably, the oscillations decay over time due to quantum fluctuations in the condensate.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between two distinct vertices within the subset. A neighbour-transitive code is defined as having a group action on its elements that transits through neighbouring vertices. This paper focuses on investigating configurations of these codes, particularly partial spreads, within the framework of polar and classical quadrangles.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, which exhibits notable anisotropy in its density pattern. This anisotropy is primarily due to the influence of non-uniform magnetic fields and intense radiation, which stem from a central compact object, the presence of massive star clusters, and the ongoing collision of molecular clouds. To quantify this anisotropy, a novel approach is implemented, which compares the likelihood of finding molecular cloud mass at a specific distance with the expectation of an isotropic distribution. This analysis is based on a 2D correlation function that evaluates the log of the mass ratio against the angular separation of the comparison points. By employing this method with the Spitzer Space Telescope's GLIMpse12m map at 22 $\mu$m, which covers the CMZ, we have determined the anisotropy parameter to be approximately 0.4, which indicates a moderate to strong anisotropy. This parameter varies across different locations within the CMZ and reveals a notable increase towards the zone's center.

A mathematical model that relies on a system of ordinary differential equations was developed to describe the time-dependent behavior of a material's electronic population distribution following intense ultrashort X-ray pulses. This model, which treats all electrons in a material equally and is based on a simplified version of the Boltzmann equation, was specifically designed for use with density functional theory. Its accuracy was demonstrated through comparisons with comprehensive first-principles simulations, and further validation was achieved by creating a comprehensive database that includes simulations for various elements, compounds, and molecules under a range of X-ray fluences. Two new analytical methods were developed to improve the model's computational efficiency: an approximation based on linear least-squares optimization and a direct solution approach that utilizes Kepler's triangle rule.

This research introduces a low-power CMOS temperature sensor that operates within a wide range of temperatures (from 40{\deg}C to 125{\deg}C). The sensor utilizes a binary-weighted resistor string and a reference voltage generator to convert temperature into a digital format, with a resolution of 0.24{\deg}C. The critical components of the temperature-to-digit converter are two feedback transistors, which utilize active load networks to enhance input voltage sensitivity. The proposed design achieves an accuracy of $\pm$1.4{\deg}C across the specified temperature range and incorporates several power-saving features, including a 10-bit digital counter, with a total static power consumption of 1.35nW and 1.06nJ per conversion cycle.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and has received considerable attention in recent decades. Heralded generation of entanglement is particularly significant, as it enables the creation of entangled states based on the measurement of a previous particle. This study introduces a novel method for producing polarization entanglement between two photons using a quantum logic gate called "quantum scissors." This entanglement production technique is notable for its high efficiency of entanglement generation, as well as its adaptability to integrate multiple optical components and control methods.

This paper investigates the concept of online Euclidean spanners in more than two dimensions. It presents two novel algorithms for constructing online (1+ε)-approximate Euclidean spanners in R^d spaces, where the number of dimensions (d) can be greater than two. These algorithms guarantee a (1+ε)-approximation factor and operate within O-dealsperation complexity, where the exponent is independent of ε. Notably, one of the proposed algorithms is also suitable for applications involving moving points and maintains the (1+ε)-approximation factor.

In the context of IoT, data acquisition from various devices poses a crucial challenge, primarily due to discrepancies in data quality and the operational constraints of sensing capabilities. Selective feature extraction is a critical strategy for addressing data variability issues, but current methods often disregard the distinct sensing characteristics of IoT devices, leading to inefficient resource utilization. To mitigate these limitations, we introduce an innovative framework that leverages IoT device features and their associated costs to optimize data usage. This is achieved by developing an optimization algorithm based on reinforcement learning, which identifies the most information-rich features while minimizing sensing expenses. Our approach is pragmatic, realistic, and applicable to real-world IoT scenarios, as evidenced by our experiments using actual data from UCI and SICK datasets.

This study introduces novel algebraic and relational structures to represent Godel modal logics. We initially present a class of Godel modal algebras, built upon bipartite lattice ordered sets, whose complex algebras of finite height mirror the finite canonical sequent calculus. We then establish an equivalent class of relational Godel modal frames, comprising bipartite ordered structures with finite height, whose corresponding complex algebras inductively mirror the finite canonical proof systems. We further extend and generalize these findings to four modal logics based on Godel's, specifically to their positive and negation extensions, as well as to their respective non-associative versions.

This research investigates the word alignment challenge in zero-shot and few-shot machine translations. We demonstrate that pre-trained language models naturally capture word-level connections across bilingual dictionaries and texts, but their alignment performance is significantly influenced by vocabulary size and alignment data quality. To enhance alignment, we propose incorporating external bilingual resources, such as dictionaries and parallel corpora, and develop a simple yet effective strategy to do so. This involves calculating aligned word probabilities using external sources and incorporating them into alignment models via self-supervised pre-training or fine-tuning. We have tested our approach with various bilingual configurations, including two low-resource languages and a high-resource language for comparative analysis. The experimental outcomes indicate that leveraging external bilingual data can substantially improve word alignment accuracy in few-shot and zero-shot translations.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures.

The theoretical existence of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) as a potential source of dark matter is intriguing, and if detectable, they can be tracked through specific stellar disruptions caused by their gravitational pull. The tool PopSyCLE has been developed to simulate these stellar disruptions in diverse PBH scenarios, and in this document, the software's details and a detailed guide on employing it are presented. Furthermore, multiple test cases are provided to facilitate the utilization of PopSyCLE in analyzing various PBH-based dark matter hypotheses.

We investigated systems of simulated hard wedge-shaped molecules, where each molecule consisted of two connected balls of different sizes, in a two-dimensional space, using Monte Carlo simulations. As the smaller ball was reduced in size, various phases formed spontaneously, starting from an unordered phase with random molecular orientations. This phase transition into a uniformly aligned phase with a specific molecular orientation occurred through an intermediate phase characterized by random molecular orientations but with a specific nematic-like symmetry breaking, specifically in the form of splay deformations.

Recurrences in the form of autoregressive processes are highly useful in modeling random fields, especially for simplifying statistical inference and understanding the relationships between functions. We develop new one-step autoregressive recurrences for stationary Gaussian processes on the sphere by utilizing a specific matrix decomposition of the covariance operator. The uniqueness of these recurrences is guaranteed under a certain covariance operator condition. The band matrix size of the recurrence determines the maximum order of the algebraic polynomial equations used to generate the recurrences, and it is essentially driven by the spectrum of the covariance operator. The degree of freedom in the recurrences is related to the eigenvector decomposition of the covariance operator, which allows for the representation of the recurrences in terms of spherical harmonic coefficients. The uniqueness and existence of these recurrences rely on the same covariance operator condition.

A conventional imaging technique relies on an optically thick screen to achieve a sharp focus, but this method involves using a large number of undetected photons. In this study, we utilize a quantum interferometric approach that requires only a thin, single-pixel screen and a small number of undetected photons to demonstrate the capabilities of a quantum-limited imaging system. Our experiment successfully demonstrates the ability to remotely alter and retrieve information about a point object's position, with the object's remote state being determined without detection.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, a phenomenon extensively observed but only partially explained. This study investigates the impact of surface roughness on dry liquid foams, focusing on the roughness characteristics that maximize friction. Our findings reveal that extremely small-scale roughness is capable of producing the highest friction, a phenomenon not fully understood. This research also uncovers a previously unidentified hysteresis in the frictional behavior of these surfaces.

This study introduces an innovative deep learning approach to skin cancer
classification, with a focus on training robust models to handle unusual skin
images effectively. Both skin and non-skin images were included in the dataset,
with the aim of developing a model capable of identifying images that may
contain cancer and are correctly labeled. This is crucial because mislabeled data
can compromise model performance and reduce its accuracy. A unique data
preprocessing technique utilizing entropy was employed to flag and exclude any
images that may contain errors in the annotation, thereby preventing them from
negatively impacting the model's training. This was achieved by identifying and
excluding images with low entropy, as these images contain distinct features and
are likely non-outlier, normal samples. In contrast, images with high entropy
indicate disorder and uncertainty in the data, suggesting potential outliers.
This approach was integrated with a pre-trained convolutional neural network
utilizing transfer learning to classify images into normal and abnormal (including
different types of skin cancer). Experimental results demonstrated that the
 proposed method outperformed traditional data augmentation techniques and
yielded improved accuracy of 94.4% compared to 92.5% for the standard approach
on the ISBI 2017 challenge dataset.

We performed high-resolution ARPES measurements on sodium and found that its electronic properties exhibit nearly-free-electron behavior with minor corrections. We also observed that the electronic relaxation time is directly proportional to the modulus of the wave vector and evaluated the self-energy correction under consideration of both intraband and interband scattering mechanisms. Based on our measurements, we estimated that the electronic relaxation time is approximately 13 femtoseconds. We validated the underlying relaxation model, which accounts for electron-scattering via phonons, using recent measurements of thermal conductivity in sodium. We also calculated the density of phonon states near the equilibrium point and discovered that these results agree well with existing theoretical predictions.

Building on previous research, where we developed a method to calculate distribution functions without relying on microcanonical ensemble simulations, in this work, we demonstrate the application of this approach to the isothermal and free expansion processes. Despite the challenges posed by changing phase space volumes, our method successfully determines the final distribution function for the free expansion process, enabling the calculation of key thermodynamic properties. To overcome the issue of changing volumes, we employ a trick involving the application of a fictitious potential. This concept can also resolve the issue of evaluating time-averaged properties in nonequilibrium conditions. Furthermore, our results obtained using this method are compared to those achieved through nonequilibrium simulations, revealing excellent agreement.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we analyze a key symmetry characteristic in the curvature weights.

We investigate solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially 
small amplitudes, in two precompressed systems: a diatomic granular chain and the 
woodpile chain. The governing equations for these solitary waves include terms 
involving strain, kinetic energy, and interaction forces, with the woodpile chain 
further simplified by a particular arrangement of masses and springs. To identify 
parameters influencing nanoptera behavior, we analyze solutions in the limit of 
vanishing nonlinearities, revealing that certain model parameters dominate their 
behavior. Moreover, we show that nanoptera in both the diatomic and woodpile chains 
can develop a localized gap in the interparticle distance, whereas the force 
between masses does not become excessively large.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, which typically involves observing signals resulting from the decay of these massive particles. In our investigation, we consider the impact of primordial features that produce massive fields, which persist throughout inflation and subsequently decay into standard model particles. We have found that the standard cosmological collider signals are supplemented by an additional peak at lower energies, which may offer a direct indication of the initial primordial feature. Moreover, we identified conditions under which the ratio of the amplitudes of the two peaks can be precisely determined, and potentially serve as a smoking gun test for the existence of primordial features.

Consider a graph of even order and its quotient obtained by removing a perfect matching, resulting in a new graph with half the original order. Under specific conditions, if this quotient has a Hamiltonian cycle, the original graph will also have one. We've identified a unique family of graphs where this relationship holds, characterized by a particular structure and a perfect matching that can be easily identified. Additionally, we've established the maximum number of independent edges in this graph framework and determined the exact number of edges in a maximum matching. Furthermore, we've precisely calculated the chromatic number of this graph framework, contradicting previous proposed upper bounds.

We employ the quantum-classical correspondence principle and the scaling hypothesis from quantum field theory to derive and experimentally verify the scaling laws governing the survival probabilities of three-state quantum walks. Specifically, our findings align with the general scaling laws applicable to two-state quantum systems.

We investigate the characteristics that enable self-supervised vision transformers (ViTs) to excel. Contrary to convolutional neural networks, ViTs utilizing large-scale datasets and intricate large-scale patch schedules are more effective in a variety of tasks. Moreover, by employing a larger transformer without a permutation invariance constraint, ViT gainfully leverages positional information, with the signal further enhanced when the patch schedule changes. Furthermore, ViTs benefit from the favorable propagation of positional cues across adjacent patches.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed to describe both dark matter and dark energy using a single fluid with dissipation and radiation. The model includes a cosmologically relevant equation of state based on the Kunz-Bergström-Lidsey equation of state for a unified fluid, which can be expressed in terms of the fluid's radiation and dissipative components. The model assumes that the fluid's pressure is a function of the space-time's dissipation and radiation, which leads to a complex expression. However, the model behaves realistically when these components are small. The equation of state for this dissipation-dominated and radiation-dominated matter is simplified, becoming similar to the equations for the cosmological constant and dust, respectively. The model's dissipation-dominated matter is characterized by a decreasing energy density similar to the Hawking state, while radiation-dominated matter is characterized by a constant energy density. The model is consistent with the current data on the cosmic equation of state and energy density, which suggests that a specific combination of dissipative and radiation components is required for a proper understanding of the dark energy density.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Generative models like the diffusion model excel at creating realistic images but often struggle to produce artwork with meaningful semantic content.
This limitation stems from the underlying generative process, which involves progressively discretizing noise and ignoring existing pixels.
To overcome this, we introduce a novel learning strategy for the diffusion model, which favors exploring latent spaces that correlate with semantic content.
Our approach builds on the concept of stable points in latent space and develops two artistic techniques:'sketch decoupling' and'style propagation.
Sketch decoupling enables the separation of latent space into independent sections, allowing for the manipulation of individual sketch vectors to generate images with distinct semantic characteristics.
Style propagation, on the other hand, enables the spread of a preferred style throughout the latent code, leading to the production of high-quality, semantically consistent images.
Ultimately, our method demonstrates the diffusion model's potential to create visually appealing and semantically rich artwork.

Recent research has shown that artificial neural networks, particularly those trained on image classification tasks, can be leveraged to create a reversible steganographic method that allows original images to be accurately recovered even after secret data is embedded. This study builds upon previous Bayesian deep learning approaches by applying Bayesian regression to a network initially trained for classification. However, our experiments indicate that this method frequently fails to produce a reliable predictive distribution for the original image, resulting in a lower steganic capacity as a safety precaution. Conversely, utilising a network trained with predictive learning achieves higher steganic capacity while maintaining comparable reversibility. Predictive learning trains a network to predict the original image given the modified version, enabling the incorporation of uncertainties in the predictive distribution to enhance steganic capacity.

The $J/\psi$ particle decaying into invisible particles is used to investigate lepton-flavor violating neutrino interactions and dark matter scavenging. The search for this process at the BESIII experiment provides the present limit of branchings and lepton-flavor violating neutrino interaction rates. It also yields the largest restriction on the dark matter density destroyed by lepton-flavor violating interactions, a phenomenon previously absent in effective field theories. Additionally, the experiment sets the most stringent constraints on sum of neutrino masses and on certain $J/\psi$ dark matter annihilation modes.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points with sizes around 1-10 kilometers, strongly indicating the presence of extremely strong magnetic fields. These features are observed using advanced techniques such as the Hartmann-Shaw technique and are found to exhibit rapid changes in location and orientation. Previous studies analyzed the distribution of magnetic bright points in time and demonstrated the presence of a power-law with an exponent of two for the number of occurrences per unit area, but the underlying causes of this power-law are still unclear. In this study, we examine the relationship between the areas and lengths of the magnetic bright points and find that their distributions are bi-component, comprising a smaller component and a larger one. The smaller component accounts for approximately 30% of the total. The two components exhibit similar skewness, indicating that the larger component is the result of the combination of the smaller component and other factors.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike deep networks, these videos expose distinct limitations in object, face, and action categorization abilities, highlighting the complex interplay between spatial and temporal factors in human vision.

Dark particles interacting via magnetic monopoles via a two-form exchange have a direct relationship with the observed strength of galactic magnetic fields. If the dark matter is composed of these monopoles, it's necessary that they interact with regular magnetic fields, or else the monopoles would get trapped and remove the galaxy's magnetic field. We've calculated the interaction between dark monopoles and regular magnetic fields, and found that this requires a coupling between the two. A strong coupling is also needed to explain the large-scale structure observations. Furthermore, we've found that a coupling in a specific range can resolve two long-standing issues: the galactic center's gamma-ray excess and the moon's anomalous brightness.

Predicting weather conditions more than a few hours in advance is a complex challenge due to the inherent unpredictability of weather patterns. This task is crucial in various sectors, but current state-of-the-art models, which leverage the capabilities of transformer networks and multi-scale spatiotemporal convolutional operations, still fall short in weather forecasting. Specifically, they struggle to accurately predict weather patterns beyond a certain timeframe of around 2 hours. This study aims to address this limitation by introducing an advanced transformer network design that utilizes a shifted window cross-attention mechanism. This innovative approach enables the model to focus on both spatial and temporal correlations in weather pattern prediction. The proposed model, called SWCA-Net, features a hierarchical attention structure that facilitates the aggregation of weather feature maps across different scales and time periods. The internal elements within each hierarchical component are arranged to perform shifted window cross-attention, allowing the model to capture both local and broader weather patterns. The proposed model also employs a temporal attention mechanism to combine weather predictions made at successive time steps. The extensive evaluation of SWCA-Net on three weather datasets demonstrates its superior performance compared to existing models, with a significant improvement of over 300% for hour-3 weather forecasting.

In models featuring three Higgs doublets, a unique symmetry can be achieved by utilizing the $S_3$ group, which has two distinct, one-dimensional representations and one ramified one. By combining a pseudo-Goldstone boson from the broken $S_3$ symmetry with a $Z_2$ symmetry, researchers have devised a method to create dark matter candidates. Specifically, they have examined the cases of both the pseudo-Goldstone boson and the elementary fermions, designating them as dark matter candidates in this study. Following the breaking of the $S_3$ symmetry, the three Higgs bosons acquire masses, while the dark matter candidates remain isolated, resistant to decay. By selecting an appropriate $S_3$-breaking scale, researchers have demonstrated the feasibility of aligning dark matter masses, in line with naturalness criteria. Ultimately, dark matter detection prospects are analyzed, with future experiments such as the XENONn1+ being potentially capable of differentiating between the two proposed dark matter candidates.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transport is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched networks within neurons, where disruptions contribute to various neurological disorders. The neuronal cytoskeleton serves as a transportation system, comprising of microtubules and associated vesicles and organelles. By formulating a minimization problem subject to optimal control equations, including transport equations along microtubules and nonlinear dynamics for organelles, we aim to optimize transport efficiency. The adjoint system, comprising of similar transport equations with adjoint coefficients, along with a cost function, helps to determine optimal parameters for microtubule lengths and organelle sticking probabilities. We utilize the finite element method for numerical solutions and solve the resulting nonlinear optimization problem through successive quadratic programming.

In understanding banking's complex transaction network, the term "NeMo' is used to describe regular patterns or clusters that emerge in the matrix representation of these interactions. These patterns, known as network motifs, offer insights into the underlying structure and can provide qualitative explanations for observed regularities. This work aims to identify such NeMo's through network motifs and explore their meanings within the context of banking transactions.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted when a white dwarf orbits a black hole. We consider two scenarios in which the white dwarf loses its mass due to the black hole's tidal forces. If the white dwarf's mass is between 0.05 and 0.25 solar masses, and the black hole has a mass similar to the sun, we find that the system's evolution leads to the emission of distinct gamma-ray bursts and microwaves. This mass range produces the most energetic and luminous radiation, including gravitational waves in the frequency range of 10^-16-10^-14 Hz. We also investigate the possibility of observing this process using the Zwicky Transient Facility.

A parametrized family of similarity measures, referred to as the Tversky family, has been developed with parameters $s$ and $t$ lying within the range of (0,1), with the special cases of the Jaccard distance occurring at $s=1$ and $t=0.5$. The inverse of this family, known as the Tversky similarity, has also been defined and it exhibits behavior similar to the normalized normalized information distance when $s$ approaches 0 while $t$ approaches 1. This family shares a unique property in comparison to the Kulcuiskii-Dinevski similarity measure.

A motion deblurring method is proposed that utilizes a data-driven approach, leveraging a synthetic blur generator to differentiate between human and scene elements. This unique technique allows for the deblurred output to be controlled through an image blur mask, enabling the recovery of moving subjects or background as desired. Notably, our method exhibits efficient runtime performance, with a processing speed of 0.04 seconds for processing even high-resolution images. Such a mask can be employed in various applications to produce human-focused deblurred images. Moreover, our method's performance is capable of adaptation for video deblurring without additional modifications. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method by comparing deblurred results with ground-truth human movement, as well as through quantitative assessments on both the EPFL Dataset and a custom human-centric blur challenge.

Synthetic molecular circuits have the potential to significantly boost the efficiency of artificial systems by allowing them to operate within harsh environments where conventional electronic components fail. A key feature of artificial intelligence is the learning neuron, and emulating its function in synthetic circuits could greatly expand the scope of artificial intelligence into physically demanding situations. Despite the capabilities of digital microchips, the development of molecular circuits capable of complex functions like learning are still largely theoretical. Prior work on molecular circuits has focused on basic logic and feedback mechanisms, but there hasn't been much work on more advanced, dynamic behaviors like those seen in learning neurons. 

In our study, we've designed a detailed model of a learning spiking neuron using digital logic and we've successfully translated this model into a synthetic molecular circuit. The molecular circuit utilizes reversible interactions and can operate in a chemically-driven logic gate environment. This circuit showcases a complex behavior with multiple feedback loops and dynamic changes in its response, and it's the most sophisticated molecular circuit yet designed.

We examine the interval chains within ultrapowers of ordered sets, specifically exploring when these interval chains form a complete set. Our analysis indicates that for a countable ordered set, its ultrapower using an infinite countable index has the capacity to contain both an incomplete and complete subset of interval chains. Interestingly, this behavior is not isolated to countable sets, as we have found examples among finite sets with a specific property.

Despite the vast number of deep neural networks (DNNs) in use, creating a general 
optimization profile for all datasets is a challenging task. Different datasets have 
distinct characteristics in terms of input values, which in turn affect the behavior 
of DNNs during computation. However, current optimization methods lack consideration 
for the data they are working with, leading to subpar performance. In this work, 
we introduce the concept of dataset-specific profiling, proposing an adaptable 
framework that allows for more accurate and efficient optimization. By profiling 
each dataset individually, rather than relying on one standardized approach, 
we can obtain precise and relevant optimization parameters. This enables a 
specialized search routine, not only leading to better results but also reducing the 
computational cost involved. Our framework also offers a practical solution for 
obtaining dataset-specific activation statistics, solving the problem of static 
parameters that fail to account for changing input values. In our experiments, 
we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various image classification 
benchmarks, achieving a substantial improvement in inference latency without 
compromising accuracy.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by a proposal from Raspaud and Zhu, suggesting that a substructure with this property, occurring within a specific graph, should itself exhibit a complete subgraph with the same number of vertices. This more robust form of the Hadwiger conjecture has been thoroughly verified for graphs with 4 colors, and the validity of it for 5-color graphs remains to be proven.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized correntropy, focusing on an aspect that previous studies have overlooked - robustness. The proposed GCR-GKL algorithm leverages the generalized correntropy with a Gaussian kernel and incorporates kernel width adaptation to optimize recovery performance. By adopting an alternating directional binary search and kernel width adaptation, the algorithm enables efficient recovery of smooth signals even in the presence of significant noise levels. The proposed method achieves this while maintaining low computational complexity, making it suitable for real-time applications. The performance of the GCR-GKL algorithm is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments across various scenarios.

We present a novel technique using entangled spinor interferometry to create customized quantum states, utilizing a noisy beam-splitter interaction followed by a projection measurement on one of the spin degrees of freedom. This method enables the production of distinct quantum states, specifically $\vert 1,\pm 1\rangle_F$, $\vert 2,\pm 1\rangle_F$, and $\vert 3,\pm 1\rangle_F$, even in the presence of noisy final state projections. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of common experimental source noises and demonstrate that our proposed method remains resilient against them.

We establish sharp inequalities for the first eigenvalue of the Robin problem associated with a given nonlinear elliptic operator, specifying particular conditions on the boundary and a homogeneous $L^q$ norm. Our analysis leverages recent findings on function and operator inequalities, as well as nonlinear elliptic equations and their first eigenfunctions.

Deep Neural Networks have emerged as a prominent technique in modern machine learning for processing complex data representations. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are particularly well-suited for applications involving structured or semi-structured data. Despite their effectiveness, the theoretical foundations of GCNNs remain complex and difficult to grasp for many practitioners. This paper seeks to alleviate this challenge by drawing a parallel between GCNNs and a traditional matched filtering approach from signal processing. By doing so, we aim to offer an accessible and intuitive understanding of GCNNs, highlighting their underlying principles and potential limitations.

Despite recent advancements in dependency parsing, insufficient resource settings pose a long-standing challenge for NLP researchers. A novel, self-training based approach combined with a sophisticated neural model is presented in this paper, aiming to enhance dependency parsing performance in data scarce conditions. The proposed method integrates a dependency parser and a language model by initially utilizing the parser to generate predicted dependencies for a portion of the available training data, then employing these predictions alongside the corresponding sentences as additional training examples for the parser. A contextualized auto-regressive decoder with the ability to capture contextual dependencies and capture long-term dependencies is used in this paper. Experimental results on six languages with varying levels of resource availability demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, which consistently outperforms the baseline models and shows significant, in some cases nearly complete, closure of the parsing performance gap relative to models trained on richer data sets.

We've used the standard light-front quark model to study the transition form factors of $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ transitions ($\ell = e, \mu, 	au$). Our approach differs from previous LFQCD calculations by fully incorporating the momentum of the light diquark, applying a correct light-front quantization procedure, and utilizing a suitable Lagrangian. As a result, our study confirms that higher-order corrections significantly impact the radiative decay constant of the charm meson, and a re-evaluation of $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ transition form factors is now possible. Given the updated form factors, we've estimated branching ratios for several $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ decays, including $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ ($\ell = e, \mu, 	au$), and have compared them to experimental data and other theoretical predictions, such as those based on QCD factorization theory.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

We demonstrate in this research that Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs can be solved via a logic system known as choiceless polynomial time, featuring symmetric circuit logic. This finding builds upon a prior discovery linking CFIs to Cai-Furer-Immerman structures, a concept introduced by Pinchasi and Sattath. Our solution involves creating a choiceless polynomial time definition on a specific undirected graph connectivity property, utilizing a symmetric circuit that can navigate both edges within the same graph and its supergraph. This finding further shows that CFIs fall under the category of properties that can be expressed using a specific type of symmetric circuit known as Q-circuits, as defined by Bullinaria and Bulatov.

A key factor in generating topological phases in 5d transition metal oxides is considered to be the proximity to a quantum phase transition of the Jefferson or Kondo type. The study of this phenomenon in the pyrochlore iridates series, specifically (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir2O7, allowed researchers to explore its insulator-to-metal transition and the resulting changes in electronic properties. Utilizing hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (HXPES), the researchers measured key properties such as work function, and the energy positions of core levels and valence bands. Their findings indicated that Bi x-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) and HXPES results track each other and suggest that the increase in Bi concentration drives a significant shift in the energy position of the Ir 5d bands. This shift is consistent with the observed changes in work function and is attributed to the increased influence of Bi doping on the local Ir environment. The data also reveal that Bi doping introduces a significant amount of disorder in the system, as evidenced by increased spectral broadening in HXPES results.

Consider a metric space equipped with a point $x_0$ and a set-valued mapping $f$, which maps this space to the space of closed unit disks in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, for example. The mapping $f$ is said to be Lipschitzian if there exists a positive real number $K$ such that for any two points $x$ and $y$ in the space, the condition $d(f(x),f(y)) \leq Kd(x,y)$ holds, where $d$ represents the distance between the points. The set of points where the mapping $f$ has a unique tangent plane at each point is denoted by $L(f)$. This set is known as the core of the mapping $f$ and it contains all the points where the mapping $f$ is a Lipschitzian set-valued mapping. It has been proven that the core of the mapping $f$ is a subset of all the points where the mapping $f$ is a single-valued Lipschitzian function. This result holds without any additional assumptions. Furthermore, it has been proven that if the mapping $f$ is a Lipschitzian selection of a set of closed convex non-degenerate polyhedra defined in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, then the core of the mapping $f$ contains all the points in a neighborhood of $x_0$. This result holds without any additional assumptions. It has been observed that if

We examine a chance process in which the occurrences of four events, labeled A through D, create a condition where A is more likely than B, B is more likely than C, C is more likely than D, and D is more likely than A. Our analysis reveals that this sequence is impossible, with the probabilities of events A through D constrained by the conditions a + b + c + d = 1 and a > b > c > d. We explore the analogous issue in two-dimensional space, investigating the criteria under which the interactions among four points A, B, C, and D satisfy the inequalities AB > BC > CD > DA and BD > DC > CA > AB. This problem can be visualized as determining the allowed configurations of points in a 2D space.

Configurable systems are versatile, yet their performance suffers due to the time and resources required to adjust their settings, often leading to suboptimal solutions. A novel approach, known as SPOT, enables compile-time optimization of a system's configuration space, allowing for a reduced search space to be explored at run-time. Our SPOT framework comprises three core components: a configuration profiler, a machine learning predictor, and an automated generator. Through an exploratory study involving three practical scenarios, we investigated the challenges and benefits of SPOT. The results indicate that SPOT can yield substantial run-time performance gains, but poses difficulties due to the intricacies of configurable systems and the diversity of valid configurations. To overcome these hurdles, we have identified several paths for future research and further development.

A new model for directly detecting light dark matter in gram-scale, underground facilities involves having it interact with nuclei, causing the released high-energy electrons to kick other electrons, known as Cherenkov electrons, in a material with a low refractive index. This process can detect dark matter interactions even when the original nuclear interaction is below the threshold for emitting visible light. Due to improved detection techniques and more comprehensive data analysis, the current direct detection experiments are now capable of constraining a broad range of sub-GeV dark matter cross-sections, including values previously considered as effective coupling constants.

This study examines the dynamics of a two-level atom interacting with a two-mode quantized electromagnetic field in the absence of any initial entanglement, using a context function to analyze the atom-field system from a quantum information perspective. Our analysis reveals the emergence of Rabi oscillations, entanglement, and a decline in quantum capacity of a quantum channel, along with the development of an entanglement-binding channel and the failure to achieve perfect quantum teleportation, all in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model. Furthermore, our research identifies the conditions necessary for the occurrence of Rabi oscillations and entanglement formation.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warning for cardiac conditions, but identifying specific peaks in these signals can be challenging when they are distorted by noise or other factors. Previous studies have used machine learning models to improve peak detection, but most of them have focused on acute beat analysis and ignored the relationship between adjacent beats. Our research introduces a new, detailed algorithm for detecting peaks in ECG signals using ECG2PND, a neural network-based inter-Beat-to-Period-Noise-Distance model. This innovative approach recognizes the significance of relationships between adjacent beats and employs a novel distance metric to optimize peak selection, resulting in higher accuracy rates when tested on the MIT-BIH database arrhythmias. Compared to other models, the Tiramisu-based method demonstrated improved performance, with an overall accuracy of 97.71% and a low error rate of 0.81%.

We analyze active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles, an active matter model in which a particle undergoes a liquid-like motion influenced by a random force and a nonlinear damping force that depends on the particle's velocity, as studied by Loiudice et al. in "Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics" [J. Chem. Phys. 149, 054501 (2018)]. Utilizing the maximum entropy method and the fluctuation theorem, we examine the probability distribution of work done by a harmonic potential on this active particle and find that this distribution deviates significantly from a Gaussian pattern, particularly in equilibrium where this deviation was previously reported by Mehl et al. in "Nonequilibrium active scalar" [Phys.
